extracted.intended_audience: legal professionals, news agency executives, journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations governing news-agency membership, permissible methods of gathering and distributing news, and evidentiary indicators of unlawful appropriation (as presented in the Associated Press v. International News Service affidavits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership duty to take service and furnish local news (Article VIII §3)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each member shall take the news service of the corporation and publish the news regularly in whole or in part, in the newspaper named in his certificate of membership. He shall also furnish to the corporation all the news of his district, the area of which shall be determined by the Board of Directors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are required to subscribe to the service and to supply the corporation with all news of their assigned district; this establishes who has contractual entitlement to local news collected by a member newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on furnishing member-required news to non-members (Article VIII §7)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No member shall furnish or permit any one to furnish to any one not a member of this corporation, the news which he is required by the by-laws to supply to this corporation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members may not give or allow others to give the news they are obliged to supply to the association to any non-member (i.e., supplying a rival news service or non-member paper is forbidden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized methods of gathering news (independent investigation; use of agents and interchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the general practice of The Associated Press to gather its news "through its own agents and through interchange with news agencies abroad with which it has relations, and through its own members;" and "any despatches it sent out were based upon its own investigation and were the product of its own enterprise and labor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP correspondents should rely on their own agents, member-provided material, and authorized interchanges; they are not authorized to appropriate rival agencies' dispatches as their own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of correspondents to report rumors/current reports for independent investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the custom for correspondents and representatives of The Associated Press, upon learning in any way of a rumor or current report, "to notify the Association of the fact in order that the Association might independently investigate it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a correspondent learns of possible news (even rumors), the correct procedure is to report it so the agency can investigate independently rather than republishing or retransmitting another organization's dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using rival or non-member despatches in preparing AP reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents and representatives "have not been authorized to use the news despatches, either in whole or in part, of any rival or competing news-gathering association, or of any newspaper not represented by membership in The Associated Press."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP material must be based on AP investigation; copying or incorporating rival despatches into AP dispatches is forbidden by policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible correspondent appointments in member newspapers (open, approved, paid arrangements)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the custom for The Associated Press to select representatives in the offices of newspapers published by its members who shall act as correspondents and supply to The Associated Press such news gathered by said newspapers; "in cities where such service makes sufficient demands ... they are paid ... with the full knowledge and approval of their employers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointing and paying a correspondent embedded in a member newspaper is permissible if done openly and with the member employer's knowledge and approval; by-laws also provide such correspondents free access to the member's news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on secret/surreptitious agreements to supply member news to rivals
rubrics_metrics.description: It was improper that B. E. Gushing "entered into a surreptitious agreement and employment to serve the International News Service with the local news of Cleveland and the news received by the Cleveland News from The Associated Press" — such secret arrangements violate the relation owed by members to the AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret employment or clandestine arrangements by a member paper's employee to funnel member-obligated news to a non-member service violates membership obligations and by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of appropriation: inspection/reading/copying of AP Markrum/spindle copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiants state they saw an International News Service employee (e.g., Mr. Atwood) "examining The Associated Press copy on the spindles at the copy-desk" and sometimes "made notes from this which he took with him when he returned to the rooms of the International News Service."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct contemporaneous observation of a rival's employee reading AP copy on Morkrum/Markrum machines or spindles, making notes, or carrying away extracts is presented as strong evidentiary indication of unlawful appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of appropriation: temporal precedence of rival dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: Deponents assert that certain International News Service dispatches "appeared in the service of the International News Service prior to the appearance of the earliest edition in which the Associated Press dispatches could have appeared," showing those INS dispatches could not have come from printed newspaper editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof that a defendant's dispatches were published or transmitted before any printed edition could have been the source supports inference that the defendant derived its material directly from the plaintiff's dispatches rather than from published newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted open assistance to AP correspondents vs. covert divulgence to rivals
rubrics_metrics.description: B. E. Cushing testified he "assisted the correspondent of The Associated Press" openly and with employer approval; by contrast, other testimony alleges secret communications (telephone booth, remote corner) and clandestine divulging of Associated Press dispatch contents to the International News Service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, employer-approved assistance to an AP correspondent is acceptable; secretive methods of communicating AP content to a rival (covert phone calls, secluded conversations, hidden note-taking) are indicia of wrongful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of 'clean hands' may be raised but must be addressed by complainant
rubrics_metrics.description: Section heading: "COMPLAINANT'S AFFIDAVITS RELATING TO THE 'CLEAN HANDS' DEFENSE."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may assert that the complainant acted improperly (clean-hands defense); the complainant responds with affidavits denying or explaining any alleged misconduct. The presence of this heading signals that equitable defenses will be contested by factual affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting animus-based explanations for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits reply to charges that ex-employees left with animus (e.g., statements that a resignation was voluntary and accompanied by complimentary letters), arguing such evidence rebuts suggestions of retaliatory or spiteful motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (letters, employment records) showing amicable resignation or employer praise can be used to rebut claims that an employee's later disclosures were driven by animus rather than by an agreement to supply rival services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and company responses to proven violations (expulsion, forbidding transmissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits note that the International News Service "was expelled and forbidden to transmit any news from England on October 10, 1916, and from Canada on November 8, 1916," tied to findings about misuse of Associated Press material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member associations may take enforcement actions (expulsion, forbidding transmission of certain foreign news) against services found to be improperly deriving content from the association's dispatches; such prior sanctions are presented as proof both of wrongdoing and of institutional remedies.
